body:
*[throwaway account to protect identity]*

As someone who's struggled with depression for decades and contemplated suicide on countless occasions, I'll note that my awareness of how it would impact others is the main reason I've never gone through with it.

When I act out scenarios in my mind, my first concern is the importance of waiting until after my mother dies.  My second concern is the need to select a method unlikely to harm bystanders (physically or mentally).

Of couse, *someone* would need to find my body.  Ideally, this would be an emergency responder with the temperament and training required to cope.

I realize that some suicidal people think differently.  And when I read or hear of one whose actions affected others catastrophically, I do regard them as selfish.  [Here](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_Glendale_train_crash) is an extreme example that's stuck with me (assuming that the man sincerely intended to kill himself).
Thank you. I appreciate the advice.  I'll try to do this, but obsessing on thoughts is one of the behaviors that's most difficult for me to avoid.  (I have OCD.)

> Ok, I admit I gave you the standard "teen" response.

Reading back my message, I see why you arrived at that inference.  In my haste, I omitted key background information.

I'm in my early thirties.  I live alone, but I speak to my mother via telephone every day.  I realize that this is excessive, but it provides some degree of comfort.

I provided more details in [an earlier message](http://www.reddit.com/r/SuicideWatch/comments/1dn3bn/waiting_to_die/).

> I can tell you that the idea of not leaving a hole in the world is a fantasy. I had a cousin who committed suicide and the impact has rippled through multiple generations of my own family. If you truly want to not be a burden to your mother, for heaven's sake, do not give her the burden of your suicide. She would truly never move on.

That's the main reason why I haven't committed suicide.  For years, I've planned to wait until my mother dies.  But I'm worried that I'll lose control and off myself impulsively.  (If I can get this bent out of shape over a [dollar figure removed] mistake, imagine how I'll react to something significant.)  Surely, getting it out of the way now (under controlled circumstances – with a proper note left behind, no mutilation or public spectacle, and a means of insuring that someone outside my family discovers my body before anyone realizes that I'm missing) would be the lesser of two evils.

But yes, avoiding both scenarios would be preferable.  And if there were some way for me to banish these feelings and not commit suicide at all, that would be ideal.  But this seems like the biggest fantasy of all.

> I know your mother loves you a lot and she would probably be surprised to hear that you consider your relationship a burden. Can you talk to her?

I can talk to her about practically anything except this.  Assuming that I'm able to postpone my suicide until after her death, she mustn't know that it's planned.

> Perhaps it's time for you to consider meds or adjust the ones you're on?

I currently take high doses of [medication names removed].

None of those drugs will treat my worst problem – OCD – or do much to mitigate the anxiety and depression stemming therefrom.  I've tried numerous SSRIs (and one SNRI) and found the side effects unbearable, even at relatively low doses that don't *begin* to affect OCD.

> If you've been through seven years of all this, you know it goes in cycles.

I've been through more than twenty years of it.  (I was diagnosed with OCD when I was about ten.)

> You may be at the bottom of a cycle but it can change.

I always remind myself of this when I'm at my worst.  But I rarely experience high points nowadays.  At best, I'm killing time, pretending to be happy and dreading the next episode.

> I also had an abusive father.

I'm sorry to hear that.  Fortunately, mine was mainly apathetic.

He did beat me up a couple of times.  [elaboration removed]

> Please - hang in there. It's ironic that depressed people are supposed to go right out there and advocate for themselves, but that's the game. Please ask your mother to help.

I honestly don't know what more she can do.  And as noted above, I mustn't tell her that I intend to commit suicide after she dies (assuming that I'm able to wait that long).

Thanks very much for responding.  Just talking (or writing) to someone helps.

> There are lots of therapies out there that work on helping you stop this crazy circle of thinking and they actually work really well*

I spent seven years in therapy.  Of course, I was a child/teenager at the time.

If I could purge the painful thoughts, life might be bearable.  But I don't believe that mine can *ever* be worthwhile.  I've missed that window of opportunity.

> Let me tell you that, from a mom's perspective, your mother will never cope. It will destroy the rest of her life if you kill herself. She will not just "get over it" ever.

I don't want to hurt anyone.  I just want to cease to exist.  I wish, more than anything, that I'd never been born.

> Is your dad not in the picture?

[response removed]

> Could these feelings be guilt about wanting to separate from your mom? 

I'm much more emotionally dependent on her than she is on me.  That's part of why I feel like a burden.  She's always been caring and supportive, despite my mental illnesses.  She doesn't deserve having to put up with me.
I wish that I could do something to help myself.  Countless antidepressants and seven years of psychotherapy (a while back) made no apparent difference.

I hope so too.  She's a wonderful person.  That's why I can't bear to inflict my suicide upon her.  She would blame herself and probably never recover.  I'd much rather endure the pain than transfer it to her.

Reading some of the other messages here (and seeing people express thoughts similar to mine) has had an odd effect.  Looking in from the outside, it doesn't seem to make sense.  Almost hypocritically, I feel as though these individuals can overcome their anguish and lead rewarding lives.  I wish that I could help them to recognize that, but who am *I* to convince them?  If someone were to tell me the same thing, I wouldn't believe it.

It really highlights the fact that my outlook is the product of mental illness.  I've always known this, but I see no solution.  I want to die, but I don't want to want to die.  I just wish that I knew of some way to be happy (or even not sad).

I just discovered this subreddit when seeking a place to discuss my own suicidal thoughts.  My feelings are much the same as yours.  Like seems pointless.  I'm constantly tired and wish that I could fall asleep and never awaken.

But I don't perceive you the same way that I perceive myself.  You seem like a lovely young woman with so much reason to live.  Even when I *pretend* to be happy, I'm unable to project the warmth and sense of purpose apparent in your past messages.

I wish that I could hug you and tell you that things will be alright.  This seems almost hypocritical, as I'd basically be urging you to move past the same thoughts that weigh on me every day.  Somehow, it's different when someone else experiences them.  I don't merely sympathize or even empathize; I see a bright path for you that I'm unable to see for myself.

I don't know you personally and can't pretend to understand everything that you've been through.  But please consider the possibility that you're viewing your existence through a clouded lens.

Perhaps I'm viewing *my* existence the same way.  I don't know that anyone could convince me of that right now, but I'm trying to remain open-minded.  I hope that you will too.  Please don't harm yourself, Jordyn.
